title: He should have been the next king.
paragraphs: He should have been the next king.

That was the expectation.
That was the bloodline.
That was the crown with his name already written on it.
Jonathan.
But the moment David walked into the story, everything shifted.

Songs started rising in the streets:
“Saul has slain his thousands… and David his tens of thousands.” (1 Samuel 18:7)

And with every lyric, Saul’s heart darkened.
Jealousy turned into suspicion.
Suspicion turned into violence.
A spear flew.

Not at an enemy.
At David.
And in that charged, dangerous, tension-filled palace—where loyalty was measured by silence—one man refused to play along.
Jonathan.
Pause.
Because this is where most people get it wrong.

Jonathan had every reason to turn on David.
Every reason to protect his future.
Every reason to stay quiet and let destiny remove his competition.
But instead…
He stepped in.

Scripture says:
“Jonathan… delighted much in David.” (1 Samuel 19:1)

Not tolerated.
Not endured.
Delighted.

This wasn’t political strategy.
This was covenant love.

Jonathan saw something others refused to see—
God’s hand on David.
And when you truly see God moving in someone else, you have a decision to make:

Compete…
Or protect.
Jonathan chose protection.

He spoke up when it was dangerous.
He defended David before a king consumed by rage:
“Let not the king sin against his servant David… because he has not sinned against you.” (1 Samuel 19:4)

That’s bold.
That’s costly.
That’s rare.
Because most people?
They stay silent when truth gets uncomfortable.
But Jonathan didn’t stop there.

When Saul’s hatred hardened again, Jonathan risked everything to warn David.
Signals were sent.
Arrows were shot.
Tears were shed.
“And they kissed one another and wept… until David exceeded.” (1 Samuel 20:41)
Feel that.

This is not shallow friendship.
This is love under pressure.
Jonathan knew something most people fear to admit:
David was the future king.
Not him.
Let that sink in.

The crown he could have fought for…
He surrendered.

The throne he could have protected…
He released.
Why?
Because honoring God’s will mattered more than securing his own position.
That’s the kind of loyalty heaven recognizes.
That’s the kind of humility hell hates.
But don’t romanticize this too quickly.
Jonathan’s story also exposes us.
Because if we’re honest…
We’ve all had moments where someone else’s rise made us uncomfortable.

Moments where we questioned instead of celebrated.
Withheld instead of defended.
Stayed silent when we should have spoken.
Jealousy doesn’t always shout.

Sometimes it whispers:
“Why not me?”
And if left unchecked, it slowly turns admiration into resistance.
Saul became that warning.
Jonathan became the contrast.
One fought against God’s choice.
One surrendered to it.
So where do you stand?
But here’s the deeper truth—the one that breaks through the story like light through a storm.
Jonathan is not the hero we ultimately need.
He’s a shadow.
A glimpse.
A signpost pointing forward.
Because Jonathan could only protect David temporarily.

He couldn’t stop death.
He couldn’t erase sin.
He couldn’t carry the weight of judgment.
But Jesus…
Jesus didn’t just stand between a spear and a man.
He stood between a holy God and a sinful world.
Let that hit you.
We were not David in this story.
We were closer to Saul—resistant, prideful, threatened by God’s authority.
Yet instead of destroying us…
Christ stepped in.
Not with a warning.
With a cross.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

He absorbed the wrath.
He took the blow.
He carried the punishment.

Not because we deserved protection—
But because He is love.
Jonathan risked his position.
Jesus gave His life.
Jonathan defended a friend.
Jesus died for His enemies.
That is the Gospel.
And that changes everything.

Because now the question isn’t just:
“Will you be like Jonathan?”
The real question is:
Will you surrender to Jesus?

Will you lay down your pride…
your jealousy…
your need to be seen, chosen, elevated—
And trust the King who chose the cross for you?
Because here’s the invitation:
Repent.
Turn from the Saul within—the insecurity, the comparison, the silent resistance to God’s will.
And receive the grace of Christ—the One who protects, restores, and redefines your identity.
Then rise.

Become the kind of person who defends what God is doing in others.
Who celebrates without competition.
Who stands in truth even when it costs.
Because the world has enough Sauls.
God is still raising Jonathans.

And through Jesus—
He’s still transforming hearts.
Sit with it.
Pray.
You don’t have to fight for a crown God didn’t give you.
You just have to be faithful where He placed you.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
